sensual

/SEN-shoo-uhl/ - the stress falls on SEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sensual means richly pleasing or gratifying the physical senses.

The resort's ads promise plainly sensual rewards: hot sand underfoot, cold juice at noon, and hammocks built for napping.

Example

The travel writer judges every seaside town by its sensual pleasures: the press of sun on bare shoulders, fried dough eaten hot from a paper cone, the shock of cold water on warm skin.

Sensual points at the body: pleasures of touch, taste, warmth, and ease. Its twin sensuous drifted toward art — rich colors, textures, sounds — while sensual stayed with bodily comfort and appetite, which is why ads for resorts and desserts lean on it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pleasurable: Pleasurable covers any kind of enjoyment — a good book, a compliment, a solved puzzle all qualify. Sensual narrows the field to the body: pleasures of touch, taste, warmth, and ease. Praise can be pleasurable; a hot bath is sensual.

indulgent: Indulgent is about permission: leaning into a pleasure past what is strictly needed, or letting someone else do so. Sensual is about the channel — the pleasure reaches you through the body's senses. A second dessert is indulgent; the taste of it is sensual.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

spartan: stripped of comfort on purpose

monkish: renouncing bodily pleasure altogether

Where it sits · how central bodily pleasure becomes — comfortable → sensual → hedonistic

comfortable vs. sensual: Comfortable is milder than sensual — comfort merely removes discomfort, while sensual pleasure actively delights the body.

hedonistic vs. sensual: Hedonistic goes further than sensual — sensual enjoyment savors the body's pleasures, while a hedonistic life is organized around chasing them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sens-

Root — sens-: to feel, to perceive (Latin sentire)

Suffix — -ual

Suffix — -ual: relating to

Put it together

Put it together: Sens- (Latin sentire, 'to feel') + -ual = relating to the senses. English then split one Latin root into near-twins: sensual took the body's side — appetite, warmth, taste — while sensuous (coined later, partly to escape sensual's spicier overtones) took the artistic side. Both mean 'of the senses'; the difference is which pleasures they reach for.

Word Choice

warm / indulgent

Sensual belongs to the body's pleasures — food, warmth, rest, touch — and can carry a wink, which is why ad copy loves it. Its twin sensuous (also in this unit) moved into the gallery and the concert hall: rich to the senses the way art is rich. Describe the feast as sensual; describe the painting of the feast as sensuous.
